content: Primary cancers of the central nervous system (CNS) are defined as malignancies originating in the brain or spinal cord. Although they account for only 3% of all adult cancers, these tumors are among the most challenging malignancies due to their aggressive growth, poor response to conventional treatments, and low survival rates. CNS tumors impose a significant cancer-related burden, with an average of over 20 years of life lost per patient. They are the third leading cause of cancer-related death in men aged 15 to 54 and the fourth most common in women aged 15 to 34. High-grade CNS tumors grow rapidly, often doubling in size within weeks or months. The current standard of care for high-grade tumors involves a multidisciplinary approach, including surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. Low-grade tumors, on the other hand, are often managed expectantly after surgery with a watch and scan policy, focusing on symptom management due to their slower growth rate (2-4 mm per year). However, recent evidence suggests that radiotherapy followed by chemotherapy with procarbazine, lomustine, and vincristine (PCV) significantly improves overall survival compared to radiotherapy alone. Glioblastoma, the most aggressive primary brain tumor, has a median survival of 8 to 15 months, with only 10% of patients surviving beyond five years. For low-grade gliomas, median survival ranges from 7 to 14 years. Despite advances in treatment, the prognosis for glioblastoma has not significantly improved over the past decade. The ketogenic diet (KD), a high-fat, low-carbohydrate, adequate-protein diet, was first introduced in the 1920s as a treatment for intractable epilepsy. It mimics the metabolic effects of fasting by shifting the body’s energy source from carbohydrates to fats, leading to the production of ketone bodies. These ketones serve as an alternative energy source for the brain when glucose availability is reduced. The KD has been shown to improve seizure control in children and adults with drug-resistant epilepsy and forms the basis of dietary interventions in glioma management. There are several variations of the KD, including the classical KD, medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) KD, modified Atkins diet (MAD), and low glycemic index treatment (LGIT). Each requires careful dietary prescription tailored to the individual’s nutritional needs, feeding habits, and social circumstances. Regular medical and biochemical monitoring is essential throughout therapy to ensure safety and efficacy. Preclinical studies suggest that the KD may selectively disadvantage glioma cells due to their reliance on glucose metabolism. Glioma cells exhibit higher glucose metabolism compared to normal glial cells, and glucose withdrawal can induce oxidative stress and apoptosis in glioma-derived cell lines. Furthermore, glioma cells may be unable to utilize ketones as an alternative energy source, making them more vulnerable to the metabolic effects of the KD. The KD may also enhance the immune system’s ability to target glioma tumors by reducing the expression of inhibitory ligands such as PD-1 and CTLA-4 on CD8+ T cells, thereby promoting a Th1-type immune response. Additionally, ketone bodies have neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and potentially lowering the risk of seizures. Clinical evidence on the efficacy of the KD in CNS cancer patients is limited to anecdotal case reports and retrospective series. Some studies report encouraging results, such as reduced tumor activity on imaging and improved clinical outcomes, but these findings are constrained by small sample sizes, selection bias, and lack of prospective validation. For example, a case report of an elderly glioblastoma patient treated with a calorie-restricted classical KD alongside standard therapy showed no detectable tumor tissue on imaging after two months, although the tumor recurred after discontinuation of the diet. A retrospective review of glioblastoma cases found that patients on a KD had lower mean blood glucose levels compared to those on a standard diet, even when receiving high-dose steroids. However, the KD alone may not significantly slow tumor progression, as suggested by limited benefits observed in some studies. Combining the KD with other treatment modalities, such as radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or anti-angiogenic therapies, warrants further investigation. The modified Atkins diet (MAD) has been proposed as a safer and more tolerable alternative to the classical KD for adult oncology patients. In a study of glioma patients with associated seizure disorders, the MAD was well-tolerated, with seven participants achieving improved seizure control and continuing the diet for up to 24 months. At the time of publication, all participants were alive, and survival rates for glioblastoma patients were comparable to expected median survival for their disease stage. The KD’s potential as an adjuvant therapy in CNS tumors lies in its ability to target multiple cancer hallmarks without harming healthy tissue. Preclinical studies have demonstrated improved clinical responses when the KD is combined with radiation, chemotherapy, or hyperbaric oxygen therapy. However, the mechanism by which the KD prevents seizures in brain tumor patients remains unclear, though it may involve reducing oxidative stress and ROS levels. Dietary interventions, including the KD, require significant lifestyle adjustments, such as meal preparation from simple ingredients and altered food choices in social settings. While generally considered non-toxic, the KD may have side effects in some individuals, potentially impairing quality of life. Systematic evaluation of the KD’s effectiveness and harms in treating primary brain and spinal cord tumors is needed to determine its role in clinical practice.
